reviews.text: YES! If you have played Fights in Tight spaces then you're expecting a premium turn based strategy game to match it. FITS was the best TBS fighting game out there hand down! I've decided to write this review early and keep updating it because I can tell I'll be playing this for a silly unsociable amount of time. Now I will have to stop playing endless mode on FITS max difficulty (currently hitting near level 150 lol) So far a great sequel! : The Fights - MORE enemies YES! Having to keep your other characters alive and helpful is absolutely a game changer! So much to consider... I imagine newer players may struggle, but that's what gaming is about baby ;) Weapons/Armour - You collect various types with interesting abilities. You can UPGRADE these oh my! For example do you use a shortsword that duplicates your first attack or do you go for +10 damage? A bow? Decisions decisions!!!!!!! The environment looks awesome. The walls smoothly swish downwards as you pan. (Improvement over FITS) The characters look great. So far I think improvement over FITS. The music is pumping so Improvement. Control more than one character, YES! Variety of characters, some are locked - Love it! Map - Does not feel linear IE it is not slay the spire style on the surface. You also can do side quests (they might not be obvious so pay attention to markers pointing off screen!) Enemy variety - Just keep playing and you will see new types to bring horror to your turn based choices. Excellent stuff! (I will update more as I play....) Negatives: I would like to be able to push left at the left most card to skip to the rightmost card. Probably doesn't matter to mouse and keyboard folk, but becomes annoying for joypad-ers In FITS you can feel the hits. In this less so?? Anyone else notice that, am I crazy? Perhaps it's the sound or my PC misbehaving? Edit: Credit to BadPsychic who said "Master volume: 100 SFX volume: 100 Music volume: 30 Ambient volume: 50" - This gives you more bang per hit! Enemy colours - They mainly are red which means you often have to keep checking their abilities too often (well I do because I have to think about all outcomes....weirdo). In FITs enemies had specifc colours which helped you quickly see/notice things.... Edit - Items - Not enough INFORMATION!!! For example, I was using the Quarterstaff and didnt realise it has range 2 until I was in the fight.... Or I have an item that adds a Card to the deck, but there's NO INFO on what that card does lol

谈到狭间骑士，就不得不谈到他的一个老前辈——方寸死斗，几年以前就在其他平台上玩过方寸死斗，当时就被别样的“动作”卡牌的类型给吸引住了，通过出牌构建动作，最后像电影一样击败敌人，真是太酷了。可惜由于略为硬核的难度以及叙事上的欠缺，最终没通关。 毫不犹豫的说，狭间骑士有方寸死斗的几乎所有优点，也改掉了老前辈的一些不足（大概吧），不论是难度选择系统还是额外的武器和消耗品系统，都降低了游戏的难度。而地图配上冒险一样的叙事，故事性上也有了增强。总的来说狭间骑士是一款值得一试的卡牌游戏，希望后续的开发中能越做越好。
内容算对得起售价，装备多地图大，队伍三人成行，有队友连击机制，战棋策略性是够的。 硬要说黑点就是卡池浅了点，位移和dot的流派强度差强人意，猴戏半天，到后期还是数值为王，直接otk boss。 打折再考虑吧，后面全程折磨，就算轻度模式也是痛苦大于乐趣。 7.5/10，后期正反馈做的太烂。
这么说吧，刚买就搞了个通宵，好玩得逼都开！

总体来说还行，就是有些保护任务太无语了吧，上来给人质刷在一个高伤害怪旁边，然后我离他十万八千里远，中间再拦着两个人，活活砍死他我能怎么办？而且作为一个肉鸽游戏你得给点局外成长啊，没有不说还是负提升，升级给的卡池不可能都是好用的吧？这不是污染卡池吗。还有游戏战斗副目标就是恶心人的，比如说给敌人弄到场外和敌人内讧身亡，然后敌方智能轻易不往边缘跑，你要么把边缘弄的多点，要么就给多个目标，比如一定回合之内胜利“或”给几个敌人弄到场外以及内讧身亡，我知道你是想显得玩家操作有技巧一些，但你没限制战斗回合，很多情况就是在浪费玩家时间，来回走位的垃圾时间，怪每回合的伤害都不如我自动护甲恢复，这就没意义了。我这光说不好的地方了，好的地方就是尽管有些许问题但还是好玩。
Would've preferred Space Knights in Tights, but I suppose this'll do.

I just can't believe such game exists in 2025 :( It looks like any other roguelite nowadays: you start a new run, selecting character and cards, go through the path, chosing a node from 2 or 3 variants, get some random bonuses (cards and equip) during the play. Once you die, you get some meta-progress and need to start a new run. Repeat. But this game has a little nuance - all the runs are quite identical! Every fckn time when you start the new run, you must play the same battles, with the same enemies, on the same maps, and the same goals. Even sub-quests are the same as far as I noticed. It gets better a little bit after finishing of prologue, but not much. I have played only 6 hours but already bored to play this damn prologue again and again after every death by some stupid reason*. Like the games of 80s, when you must start the game over and over again, but today is 2025, and you can find lots and lots of normal roguelites, where every run is different. This is what I would recommend to do instead of this game. * regarding stupid reasons to die. This game is bad at explaining its mechanics, and it is not always clear what will happen. My last run has ended when my warrior used dodge to negate the ranged attack, but this attack killed my main character, who stayed behind the warrior. This card says clearly that the attack does 0 damage, not that it skips the target and goes further, so how was I supposed to know that?

已全成就，这一作比起前作来说难度稍有提升，同伴能加行动力和辅助攻击，效果看上去很好，但是在高难度下没有移动卡修正会很容易陷入包围，有时候反而不如单人打起来有节奏，当然也有可能是习惯了前作的单人作战，双线通关之后只觉得隐藏线的难度其实并不如背叛线。 隐藏线进入方式： 进入隐藏线的关键就是有没有佩戴变节戒指和拒绝情报头子，如果没有变节戒指会在女爵战斗前拒绝情报头子时被包围然后戛然而止。 补充几个这款游戏里的小要点： 1，众所周知卡牌游戏不是卡越多越好，这款游戏尤其如此，请尽量把卡组保持在20-25张左右，多了会很难受，除非是低难度，自带移动卡补助。 2，高难度没有移动卡牌补助时，一定要保证自己的移动类卡牌有5张左右，推荐卡，滑行，1代就是神卡，互换，这张卡在一代没有2代作用这么明显，很多要求将敌人推击出去的奖励，突然有这么一张卡就比较容易达成了。反转，腾跃，没什么可说的，被包围时有这么一张卡真是救命。 3，辅助队友比较推荐猎人或者怪盗，可以在远距离用弓箭支援攻击，次推拳手和牧师，拳手的摔拌类卡牌都能很好控制敌人，牧师可以装备铠甲，还带灵修特性，有补血卡时可以增加融错，同类型的术士和巫师作为辅助来说太脆了。最后时几个能装备盾牌和铠甲的角色，搭配防御反击卡足够耐揍。 角色推荐： S级，术士，虽然作为辅助角色不看好，但是作为主控角色，这就是天秀角色，初期就带一张传送卡奠定位置，29级后解锁传送他人更是解决了很多任务里的被保护者的垃圾站位。闪电，魔法护甲，魔法盾都是全图选择对象使用，保护队友和任务目标非常实用，治疗全员升级后可以回复12点血，大大增加存活率。神秘推击轻松把站位不佳的远程敌人推出地图，可以说相当灵活，虽然血皮很薄，但是术士就是这么灵活好用。 A级，斗士，这是个非常厚的角色，可以同时装备盾和铠甲，护甲可以轻松堆到12点+，搭配上几张升级过的反击卡轻松在人堆里收割人头。何况还能用传奇神剑黑曜石剑，配上华丽射击卡和带易伤效果的卡，轻松打出50点以上的伤害，100点伤害的成就我就是拿斗士做的，都没用易伤就堆出128点伤害。 拳手，摔绊大师，虽然不能装备武器，但是摔绊卡非常好用，硬控绝大部分敌人，除了那些满图都是重装骑士的任务外，拳手是最不容易出错的一个，走位不好被围攻？轻松摔开一条路逃跑，缺点是摔绊不能触发同伴攻击，单人solo生存率很高。 B级，剑士，牧师，怪盗，猎人都在这里，没什么好说的，牧师虽然是灵修角色，但是初期卡牌并不怎么好，传送卡在29级和30级才能解锁，在没有解锁之前牧师做为主控和剑士没什么区别。怪盗猎人也都很脆，弓箭卡虽然有远程优势，但是别忘了这是狭间格斗，虽然不至于会小到如一代的电梯9格，可大地图也不算很多，唯一优势是可以卡桌子对付一些手短的笨蛋敌人，但是在最后2章远程敌人会带警觉，你射它还会被反射。。瞬间就不香了。 C级，巫师，怎么说呢，这个诅咒系的角色只适用单人solo并严格控制卡组，不然诅咒卡一多，却没有拿到丢诅咒卡回血或者回移动的卡，几乎瞬间会导致战斗恶化，而你要去删除诅咒类卡的话还不如回去用术士。毕竟你都已经洗掉了这个角色的特征，何况还浪费金币。总之不推荐新手玩，20级才能解锁这最后一个角色想必也是因为如此。

《狭间骑士》是一款漫画风格爬塔肉鸽卡牌玩法与硬派战棋策略玩法相结合的一款独特的游戏。玩家需要构建适合自己的卡组，并在狭小的空间中进行战斗，所有的队友共享一套卡组，但是队友数量的增加可以帮助玩家获得更多的卡牌。玩家需要在每个回合控制好行动力，进行移动攻击行为以及改变各种站位关系。因为在狭小的空间中进行战斗，将敌人直接杀死或击出场外都可以造成击杀，因此游戏的策略度很高，策略玩法也很多样。 [h1]肉鸽爬塔的关卡设计[/h1] 本作游戏在关卡推进的过程中采用常见的肉鸽爬塔的形式，玩家完成当前的关卡可以不断向前推进，并选择适合自己的路线和适合当前队伍状态的目的地。给予玩家在关卡选择上的策略性，同时玩家也可以通过战斗和商店购买一些卡牌，从而构建自己不同的卡组来改变战斗的方式，玩家也可以通过招募队友来增加队伍的战斗力，并且在战斗中使用一些辅助攻击的机会。游戏的底层逻辑还是卡牌的玩法，因此需要玩家在构建卡组的时候，花费更多的精力。 [h1]狭小空间的战棋战斗[/h1] 本作游戏的战斗形式采用卡牌的玩法与狭小空间内的战棋战斗玩法为主。游戏标题中的狭间大概指的就是狭小紧凑的战斗空间。在这样的空间中战斗，玩家的移动力收到限制，因此玩家的行动和站位就变得至关重要了。游戏的设定中，玩家将敌人生命值打掉，我是将敌人推到场地之外都视为击杀，而许多的攻击行为都是可以将敌人进行位移的。因此本作游戏中玩家的策略就变得更加多样，可以选择将难以击杀的强大敌人推出场景之外来击杀。增加游戏的策略性，同时也点明了游戏的标题。 游戏的战斗是通过卡牌和战棋玩法进行的，每个回合玩家会在卡组中抽取一定数量的卡牌。玩家回合中所有人物共用一套卡组，也共用一个回合。在玩家回合中，玩家需要打出卡牌，并选择对应的人物使用在进行移动和攻击等行为。玩家队伍共享行动值，所有卡牌的使用都会消耗数量不等的行动值。部分卡牌可以恢复行动值，人家结束会和开启下一回合也可以直接将行动值恢复满。当玩家的行动值为空无法再使用卡牌或是使用完毕手中所有的卡牌都会结束当前回合，进入敌人的行动回合。 队友的辅助攻击是游戏战斗中的一大特色，通过位移将人物推到敌我双方其他单位的攻击范围内会进行一次辅助攻击。例如玩家将远程人物放置在一个攻击的位置上将敌人推到攻击范围内就可以让队友进行一次远程辅助攻击，造成更大的伤害。近战攻击同样使用玩家在攻击一次之后可以受到队友的辅助攻击，因此包围敌人的战斗方法来得更加实惠且节省行动值。值得注意的是，敌人也会采用相同的辅助攻击的方式，不过玩家的行动中，敌人的辅助攻击会有一个回合的延迟，大家可以利用这个延迟将敌人推到敌方远程队伍攻击的范围内，让下一个回合的敌人遭受队友的攻击，从而改变战场形势，对玩家更加有利。 游戏的战斗策略度还是非常高的，运用的方式也是非常硬派传统，可玩性很高。综合来看，本作游戏我十分推荐。 [h1][quote=] [table] [tr] [th] 欢迎关注 [b][u][i]U_U鉴赏家培养计划[/i][/u][/b][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 关注U_U鉴赏家，开启精彩游戏之旅。 [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1]

Read some bad reviews here and was in doubt, but in the end I knew I had to play it as I did enjoy Fights in Tight (FITS) spaces a lot. And I am glad I did. In a way a lot of the negative reviews here have a point. You get exactly what you expect, and surely it could have been grander. But I find it way above FITS in quality, story, options, graphics, card combinations, added multiple characters played as a group, equipment, etc... Surely it is repetitive... But are not ALL games repetitive? You just got to find the repetitiveness you like. And when I complete it then I will probably stop playing this and look for something new. The amount of hours of fun I get from this make this an easy buy. But then again all to their own taste. Like Slay the Spire it requires luck in card draws and random events happening. Sometimes unlucky placement of enemies, items on map, etc.. can ruin a good run. But like slay the spire... we still restart and play again until we get that extreme joy of happiness when things work out exactly like you planned. Some cons so far is I find the UI lacking. Especially effects like dodge, rounds armour is retained, god gained from story decision the instant it happens (I check the total gold sum in map/story page). But all of this is minor nuances. I assume they will get around to improve this as it seems like extremely minor issues. The game itself functions perfectly for what they set out to make. The only question is if you also like the ideas they brought along...

在如今，肉鸽卡牌游戏早已成为游戏爱好者们茶余饭后拿来消遣的最佳选额之一，其构筑的随机性与策略的精密性让人欲罢不能。或许是想“蹭一蹭时代红利”，每年都有大量肉鸽卡牌游戏涌现出来，有简单的劣质仿品，也不乏精良之作，在这其中《狭间骑士》摒弃了传统卡牌游戏的线性套路与战棋游戏的冗长计算，转而以“狭小空间”为舞台，让玩家在有限的格子间体验无限的可能性，在同类游戏中脱颖而出。 [h1][quote=] [table] [tr] [th] 欢迎关注 [b][u][i]U_U鉴赏家培养计划[/i][/u][/b][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 关注U_U鉴赏家，开启精彩游戏之旅。 [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1] [h1]在方寸棋盘上编织卡牌的狂想诗篇 [/h1] 《狭间骑士》的设计核心可以用“限制中诞生自由”来概括，游戏将战斗舞台压缩至8x8甚至更小的棋盘，但在这方寸之间，随机性与策略性的化学反应被催化到了极致。在游戏中，玩家操控的整个队伍共享同一套卡组，初始小队仅能携带较少的基础卡，但随着新队友的招募，卡牌的上限也相应的得到了增加。和大部分肉鸽爬塔游戏一样，《狭间骑士》的一个大关由数十个节点构成，一战到底，去商店构筑升级牌组，亦或是进行血量的回复，前进路线交由玩家自由选择。 《钴蓝核心》充分利用宇宙飞船的“位移”机制，让攻击和防守玩出了新的花样，为游戏策略带来了更多的可能性，《狭间骑士》的亮点与此有着异曲同工之妙。在这里游戏的击杀机制颠覆了传统战棋的“血量至上”逻辑，无论是将敌人血量清零，还是通过击退、拉扯将其逼出战场边缘，均可达成击杀。基于此种机制，已经有玩家研究出了“台球宗师”的玩法，其核心卡牌为“弹性墙壁”、“连锁碰撞”类型的位移卡牌，或许伤害很刮痧，但效率确实出奇的高。这种玩法将战场本身转化为了武器，让每一寸地形的价值都被重新评估。 利用地形击杀敌人是本作的一大特色，“辅助攻击链”的创新性设计则是游戏的另一亮眼之处。该玩法的基础是敌人之间存在友伤现象，相比于一味的叠甲，耗费行动值利用位移类型的牌拉开与敌人的距离从而躲避攻击似乎更为可取，当玩家推开敌人1，离开敌人1的攻击范围时巧妙地将其带入友方射手的攻击路线之上，这是第一波无伤消耗；如若经过设计和安排，能够将敌人1推入敌人2攻击范围，那么玩家回合结束后便可假借敌人2之手对敌人1进行消耗，诱使其友军“误杀”队友，这种借刀杀人的策略将战棋的深度推向新的维度。基于上述的两种玩法，作为肉鸽爬塔游戏的《狭间骑士》的卡组构筑不再是单纯的数值堆砌，转而强调“战术生态位”的互补，输出系和防御系的卡牌固然能够带来最为直观的效果，即敌人血量的扣除和自身血量的保持；但看似有些鸡肋的位移系卡牌极大地丰富了游戏的玩法与深度，只要在行动前精心设计就可以实现兵不血刃的效果，好一个谈笑间樯橹灰飞烟灭。 [h1]在策略的窄门中窥见无限 [/h1] 《狭间骑士》的精妙之处在于它证明了“限制”可以是创意的催化剂，当其他游戏追求开放宇宙的辽阔时，它选择在8x8的棋盘上雕琢微观世界；当主流设计推崇角色个性化时，它用共享卡组机制书写团队史诗。这是一款为策略狂人准备的硬核盛宴，每一次位移连锁都是对物理法则的优雅嘲讽，在这片狭小的战场之上，每个玩家都能找到属于自己的无限可能。

继前作《狭间格斗》取得一定的成功之后，开发商又在前作的玩法基础上进一步拓展，将酷酷的黑白西装小人带到了中世纪，变为了一个个职业各异的冒险者。本作在完美继承前作玩法的基础上，进行了进一步的加法，游戏变得更加复杂，丰富的策略性和随机性的结合让人感到迷人。玩法随便一脉相承，但美术风格变了不少，由原来的色块小人变得更有细节，美术风格也与中世纪风格十分相称，但UI设计则略逊一筹。讲实话本作还是比较挑人的，并不推荐给每一个玩家，战棋与rogue卡牌的结合看起来很美好，但不断做加法却没办法让每个系统十分融洽的存在，以及rogue的随机性也让战棋这个本就亟需思考的玩法很容易收到挫败感，但若是对着两种玩法都十分喜欢，那本作也绝对会成为你的不二之选。 [h1][quote=] [table] [tr] [th] 欢迎关注 [b][u][i]U_U鉴赏家培养计划[/i][/u][/b][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 关注网 易U_U鉴赏家，开启精彩游戏之旅。 [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1] [h1] 美术加码，但UI迷人[/h1] 前作的纯色色块小人确实给玩家留下了深刻的印象，简单明了的同时又不失画面感。本作则改为了交叉线绘制的立体漫画风格，对于本作中世纪题材来说，表现力确实更强，尤其是对于一些法系职业，丰富的色彩让技能或者攻击表现更加出色，但游戏整体的攻击表现并不算太强。而相较于比较写实的地图，人物的颜色为了便于区分还是变为了整体一个颜色，但人物多起来就会看起来花花绿绿的，当然这一点也是因人而异。 而UI的设计则让我颇为不喜，游戏中很多信息的放置非常不明显，一些隐藏内容使得玩家需要频繁的去切换那个显示信息的按钮，信息获取非常不便，再说游戏的视角，虽然可以旋转视角，但实际游玩中不算很方便，总会有遮挡，而像一些什么超出地形的击杀也更加难以实现，有时候莫名奇妙地形杀了，换了个视角才发现那里是个门。 [h1] 战棋加Rogue＋……加得越多真的越好玩吗? [/h1] 游戏的核心玩法是卡牌rogue加战棋,简单说就是“用卡牌控制战场”,而这里的战场既是”狭间”。每回合玩家从牌库抽取固定数量的攻击、位移、防御卡等，通过消耗行动点或是连击点数打出手牌。而与前作不同，本作第一个大的玩法更新便是引入了职业分工,比如最基本的战士擅长近战推拉,术士可远程轰炸或传送，盗贼则以闪避和连击见长。理想情况下，三人小队能打出精妙配合——比如战士将敌人推至悬崖边，术士补上火球完成地形杀。 但实际体验中，职业平衡问题凸显,尤其是因为卡牌限制的存在，某一大类的卡牌只能由该大类使用。很多角色的配合看似强力，却因手牌共享机制沦为“累赘”，简单的想，想要每回合能打出不受限的最大化收益，那应该怎么选择职业，很明显最简单的方式是——全队统一职业，这样便能保证卡牌的最高利用效率，虽然这样可能不是在运气加持下的“最优解”，但却是在多数情况下的最稳妥选择。 此外，当游戏角色变多时，各角色多资源的争抢也更加明显，这也让资源分配变得十分硬核——队伍共享手牌与体力，多角色同时遇险时，常面临“保谁弃谁”的抉择，这种设计更进一步强化策略性，但也会让前期上手的挫败感加强。 而在玩家深入游玩之时，便会发现“狭间”一词的真正含义，玩家的行为被限制在一个狭小的战斗区域，也就是战棋的棋盘，虽然玩家的行为并不像传统战棋那样一板一眼，但在面对众多敌人围殴时，选择避其锋芒总是没错的，而在本作中的种种机制加成下对于位移或是击退的需求迅速上手，而这时玩家往往需要均衡的调整牌组的构成，从而最好能够打成一种伪随机，使得玩家能获得更大的概率来规避伤害，你可以说这种构筑也是Rogue卡牌乐趣的一部分，但是他显然没有获得其中真正的精髓，玩家无法从卡牌构筑中获得build的乐趣，而是使得卡牌更加均衡，来让的行动更具有预测性，多了一份战棋的严谨策略，少了一些随机构筑的乐趣。 [h1] 🔘总结🔘[/h1] [hr][/hr] [b] 总体来说，本作在前作的基础上做出了许多改进，职业分工、战棋策略与Rogue元素的结合都让游戏的可玩性得到了提升。然而，复杂的系统设计并未完全融合，职业平衡与资源分配的难度让游戏门槛变得更高，UI与视角设计也带来了一定的不便。本作确实是一部非常挑人的作品，如果你热爱战棋与Rogue卡牌的结合，能够接受一定的运气成分和策略挑战，那么本作无疑值得一试；但如果你偏好更流畅、直观的体验，那可能需要再三考虑。 [/b]

TL DR: A decent game, but worse than it's predecessor. Knights in Tight Spaces is like an undercooked, rushed sequel to the excellent Fights in Tight Spaces. There is fun to be had, but why bother when there is something better? The good: -Nice theme -Different classes to pick from with different strength and weaknesses and have class-specific cards. Just wish they leaned heavier into the rpg element here, the classes mostly have just have a few defining abilities and some class-specific cards (which are mostly traps, see below), that's it. -Multi character party management is a neat idea. I *think* the game encourages you to play with three members of the same class though, since otherwise you'll run into "oh, <this card> can only be used by <that member> but they aren't in position right now" problems more often. There aren't a lot of class specific cards either, nor are they stronger to offset that disadvantage. The classes don't even complement each other in a meaningful way. Sorry, this was supposed to be a good point. Anyway... -When your party members stand adjacent to your target after you attack it, they automatically attack them, too, which feels satisfying and offers some tactical opportunities. -Lots of different enemies The bad: -The UI in general is horrible, Camera too close to the action, enemy stats not visible without rotating the camera, sometimes it's a headache to select a square on the board because some UI element is in the way from multiple directions. Some UI elements like enemy descriptions are always on top of rotate camera buttons - probably a resolution thing, but still a sign this wasn't tested a lot. -Gameplay is like its predecessor, but more cluttered and bloated. Why do I need to read the equipment layout of enemies? For that matter, why do I need to know that an enemy deals +4 damage against supernatural enemies? Unless you can later in the game unlock an undead necromancer to your party this will never be relevant information. Why do I need to know that an enemy deals "+6 damage with weapon attacks, modify damage by +1"? I already know the total attack damage, which is all that really matters. -There is more story blibs between missions. It's not like the writing has gotten any worse, there is just so much more of it that it overstays it's welcome rapidly. -Cards are 90% recycled in name and effect from the predecessor, which is kind of funny because they were not exactly balanced then and still aren't. Feels a bit cheap and a missed opportunity to tweak some stats. At the same time, having multiple characters in your party clearly shifts balance in favor of some cards but not others. -Controls: No remapping. End turn is on "enter" so you are forced to switch hands between mouse, q+e for camera controls and tab for character controls, and Enter. No quick cast of cards by pressing 1/2/3... for cards. Overall, a lot of clicking. -Building a deck and crafting synergies feels less satisfying. Instead of permanents perks (nice and clean) you now need to equip three characters with weapons and armor that grant nice, but rather bland effects. Each party member also adds three basic cards to your deck when you recruited, muddling the pool further. -The campaign feels directionless because it gives you no sense how long it will take. Is the next mission the last or are there 50 more to go? Five hours in and judging by the achievements I'm about halfway through. Despite it's length there is also not much in the way of progress somehow. Sidegrades and minor quibbles: -Graphics are fine, not better or worse, just different. -UI: Possibly duplicate colors are assigned to your party members seemingly at random. Since some cards can only be played by certain characters, this is a missed opportunity to color-code by class. -Visually differentiating enemies: Not *all* shield bearers have the "can't be attacked from the front" perk, only the one with slightly different looking shields. Not *all* enemies with long weapons actually have range. It's not horrible, but the precesessor was clearer on the visuals here. -Some missions in the campaign have the goal "destroy 1-2 obelisks". As always, completing a sub-objective nets you some kind of reward. What happens if you don't destroy them before you defeat all enemies? Is the reward forfeit? Do you gain it regardless? Neither, actually. Combat doesn't end. You just keep punching the 50hp obelisks without any opposition or stakes. Who thought that was fun? -Map: During campaigns you visually choose missions on a map, with the next mission options always being close by. Makes sense, you travel the roads to the next location. Except suddenly you have side quests all over the country, teleporting your back and forth. Not a big deal, but then why have a map in the first place? -Some boss enemies have the description: "It's you!". No it's not. It's the boss. Nobody looked at the tooltip during testing? -If I click on a card, but realize I have the wrong character selected, the card *unselects* when switching characters, forcing me to click on it again (again, no shortcuts for selecting cards...) -Equipping party members: Equipment is neither sorted nor filtered? In fairness, it's not a lot of equipment so that isn't a problem, but it would have been nice to select an equipment slot and getting only wearables in return. -The stat info shows the last entity the mouse hovered over. Which is fine, but if you hovered over/clicked at party member A, then switched to party member B via tab, it still shows party member A, which is slightly jarring at first. -Enemies with indirect attacks (longbowmen, healers etc.) still show their target squares when stunned.

I've really been trying to like this game, and was actually succeeding for the most part. HOWEVER the number of bugs, quality of life sins, and gameplay oversights has kind of ruined it for me. For reference, I've played the first game a fair bit, and have spent an ungodly amount of time in deckbuilders. The first game was a very cool concept that was pretty well executed and the novelty kept me engaged a good while, but didn't quite have enough personality to reeeally dig the hooks in. Some might disagree, but I think the audio/visual/story aspects have all gotten a very nice upgrade from the FiTS. The gameplay changes are more a series of hits and misses. I still like the positioning system in the game, and I think having extra party members and team attacks actually adds a good deal more depth to the movement/positioning part of the game. Despite the lamentations of the whiners, I believe it does what it's supposed to do here very well. The problem with the new mechanics for me is that all your characters share a single deck, but the mechanics don't seem to support this. Adding cards for one character will usually dilute the deck for another. Without spending a tonne of time in the game, it seems like higher level play will eventually boil down to either having a bunch of characters that all do the same thing, or just taking generically strong cards and avoiding character specific synergies altogether. Ultimately it feels like they just kind of did a lazy port of the FiTS cards and systems without exploring how some more thorough changes could improve what they've brought to the table. The icing on this sad cake is the total lack of standard quality of life features present in any worthwhile modern deckbuilder. The tooltips are either lacklustre or non-existent. Playing cards between your different party members is janky, frustrating, and accidental misclicks are frequent. There's a general lack of clarity on what certain things do and how they'll interact. I was willing to forgive all these things because the novel combat system feels cool and ultimately I think it's more refined than the first. The bugs really got to me though. Many things not working as intended and then multiple softlocks killed it for me. Very disappointing!

I have enjoyed my playthrough of this game, I do realise that opinions are torn on it, but these are mine. I played Fights in tight places and loved it, I finished it several times with different fight styles and even bought the DLC for it which drew me back in for more plays. This game is similar in how it plays, but now you can gather a small crew of two additional people. This feature is a bit mixed, I love the team ups where if you have your crew positioned well, you trigger a team up attack when you perform an attack on enemies. This can be very satisfying watching the chain reaction of attacks and be greatly helpful when combating bosses or tough foes. You can have a team of mixed combat styles, some work well together, but some others give you cards that work against you leaving some of your team useless when useless cards are drawn. I suppose this essentially forces you to experiment with different crew mixes to see what works, but it can be annoying when a crews cards seem to dominate the leaders cards forcing you into either defensive or worse still unable to do anything to defend a character. I do note that as you expand your team, you also expand the cards (as noted above, but can be good with a good crew set), you also expand the amount of turns you can take in a round. If you mix magic with archers, or sometimes melee characters you can gain a card ability to heal your crew members depending on position requirements, this is a good thing that adds to the team play feature. You earn additional cards as you play just like in Fights, you also unlock new cards when completing the game, some good, some just filler and useless. While playing it is possible to remove chosen cards, but this is either at the expense of currency, or forced choice between rewards or removing cards, often you need that health, or that upgraded weapon/armour/item, so you end up with a tough choice and can sometimes be left at a disadvantage no matter what you decide. The stages can be interesting, but not always is it clear where you may be able to knock an opponent out of the level. You can rotate the view, but I found when playing on Steam Deck I could not zoom in or out like I could on my laptop using keyboard and mouse, regardless some stages are obvious where a knockout can be done, some others not so much. Also some of the areas can seem to small to move around when you have a full team, leaving you stuck and just praying you get enough attacks (or even attacks that allow close quatres combat) to defeat the nearby enemy. Overall I do like this game a lot, it has its quirks, it also does have some bugs (one time characters failed to load into a level, I restarted the level and it worked then. Another time the game stopped responding to choosing cards, so I could not proceed, I managed to resolve by exiting the game, then loading back in), it does force you into making some tougher choices, particularly when playing as a team. However it is possible to play through with only your first chosen character and not hire a crew, this can give you mixed results on being able to get through the whole game. I do recommend if you have played Fights, particularly at the sale price, I certainly got my moneys worth and will be returning again in the near future for another full play through. Players will be torn on how the game has changed from Fights, but again this is personal preference, you may like it like me, or dislike it like many others, just give it a taste for yourself.

Falls into a few key problems I have with card-based games, and doesn't give you a way to effectively manage the issues. MANY of the cards can only be used in tandem with other specific cards, or only with specific classes, or only at certain combo levels, or only at certain distances. They provide no way for you to effectively cycle through your deck to get what you need. Battles take forever as you try to extract an optimal combination of cards in the right order from a deck of half unusable cards. A lot of the time, and I mean A LOT, you end up just moving your units out of the way of attacks over and over, waiting for the right combination of cards to achieve an objective or overcome a certain obnoxious enemy. The card rewards are random and sometimes cannot even be used by your party. Most of the cards just feel like bloat. You don't get the satisfaction of building an effective deck. The game also seems to be overly obsessed with you moving enemies around to kill each other or to throw them off a cliff, which gets REALLY old when those objectives are the only way to get something useful rather than more deck-bloating garbage cards. Imagine trying to fight 6 of 7 enemies with 30 health to a hair's breadth of life, so you can try to shove them into some other enemies swing for 5 damage without accidentally killing them, only to waste a 20+ minute battle because you trigger a support attack by accident. It just becomes sooooo irritating. I'd also say the characters and classes are VERY shallow, the story is shallow, and the map is pretty uninspired. If you want a card combat game that gets it, go with Slay the Spire 2.

I have a difficult time recommending this game. It's a good game! There's fun to be had! People go out windows! It has significant flaws though. First and foremost, the addition of NPC companions really muddles the deliciously tight design of Fights In Tight Spaces. All allies work from your single hand of cards, so you will seldom be able to really make use of two or more characters. More often, you'll have one primary and then the rest are just there for the Assist Bonk, which works fine until both characters need to be moved and you will NEVER have enough movement cards for a party. This problem is compounded by just how sodding many enemies you will be facing off against. Most missions will see you facing five to six foes at the same time. If you want to stay mobile, you'll probably want to stay solo. There're some other quibbles, like whole slew of cards being locked to classes but still showing up as rewards, MUCH bigger maps, and a somewhat cluttered art style, but that'll come down to personal preference. As for positives, the addition of equipment and supernatural enemies is a nice touch and there's more meat to Events. There's still lots of fun to be had here! TL;DR - It's still a good game, but not as tightly designed as Fights in Tight Spaces. Worth a buy, just wait for a sale.

I enjoyed the game for what it was. That is to say, it's a relatively short card based TB RPG. There is not much plot, it's mostly focused on the card based battles. You do have to play through it at least twice to see the two paths through the game, and the second path with its boss rush at the end was quite fun, even if the first path was harder. Once nice thing about the game is the battles are pretty quick (under 10 minutes), so it's a nice game to play if you're taking a short breaks from something else. Enemy turns also run if you alt-tab out of the game, a feature I wish more turn-based games offered. I had some issues with randomness during my first few runs, but once I really got discriminating about the cards I kept and decreased my deck size (to about 7), it went a lot smoother. That said, the runs I lost are because the RNG didn't give me any cards to work with for my deck and the game could have been a bit more discriminating with the cards it offered. E.g. the game offered magic and archery cards to a party that had no one who could use a bow or cast magic. The opportunities to buy equipment or eliminate/upgrade cards from your deck are very limited. Effectively, you have to have a good idea what your deck will be when you start your run. There were also a few issues with character design, like the Swordsman seems to built around parrying and countering but can't wear armor, which limits his block to a value where he has to rely on dodge countering. I ran through the game both solo and with a party, I can say that having a party was easier. However, because the party shares cards, it has to be party of the same character type. I.e. you want 3 melee characters, not a melee, ranged and magic character. You want to avoid the situation where your melee character is in a position to attack and you only have magic and archery cards in your hand. This is the conundrum of the party system; a card based game like this rewards specialization, however players generally want a diverse party. I recommend this game, if you get it on sale and are looking for a title you can casually jump in and out of.

Inferior to the prequel in every single way. The style is a choice that can go either way, depending on the person, though I personally strongly prefer the previous iteration. The more detailed characters do not work that well when the enemies ragdoll, and though the levels are a lot more detailed and nicer-looking, the price is that the variety is much, much lower. The same 4-5 get recycled all the time. Not only is it tiring, but they're actually not very well designed for throwing enemies off-scenarios. And that is another thing. The enemies try a little TOO hard to avoid being anywhere close a ledge, no matter what. It might be a combination of the inferior level design, but you'll often spend 20-30 turns of just making tiny little switches so you can throw that last enemy off so you can fulfill your optional objective. Because they're not random anymore; now, it's fixed. Rather than banking on the replay value (the entire point of the game), it has a SINGLE campaign with a lot of dialogue that you must skip since you've already read. Once you finished the campaign once, you've basically done all there was to do in the game, unlike the previous entry that had so much content, so many new things to try. Because, in the previous one, there were so many nice builds and ways to exploit both the environments and characters. Here? Maybe two-three good cards per character. Equipment adds surprisingly little, making money is painful as all hell (always behind annoying secondary objectives that can have you trying the same scenario for an hour, just micromanaging everything so you can get that enemy to kill the other enemy, because it's either that or zero gold gain. Levels take much longer. The previous one was addictive because it was non-stop action. Snappy, short levels and relentless, fearless enemies you could quickly manipulate into cool combos, making you go, "Just one more!". Here? More insidious, careful enemies you have to chase a great deal of the time, which makes every single level drain you. And this game... it just is so much worse with other characters. It's tedious, it's more micro-management, it's always unsatisfying that you have cards only certain characters can use, and they must be in JUST the right position to use it, not to mention that the options are limited (most cards obviously suck and are just filler), and it makes the entire experience quite boring. Not to mention that equipping items on each character means extra clutter for your hand. The game was simply not well-thought around having such a large hand; it's not easy to find the cards you want. That is, when they work. This game has plenty of unresolved bugs that have been around forever, and it makes it feel like abandonware. From getting suck and being forced to exit levels when not a thing responds, to crashes and everything in between, it now also forever sucks. Animations are now clunkier and a lot more repetitive; less alive, somehow. With the previous one, you could kind of let the cinematic camera take you on a journey as you did sweet kung-fu moves with tons of variation, making it feel like a movie. Here? Move right. Raise sword, lower sword. Raise sword, lower sword. Turn to the left. Again. Replays are absolutely unsatisfying. And the character design. Again, a personal thing. But most of them are... plain ugly. Fine for the monsters, but who'd ever want to look like the guys we're forced to play as? There's maybe two okay ones; for the rest, it's like they TRIED to make them unappealing. They missed on every mark. Every. Single. Mark. There's not a single thing this did better than Fights in Tight Places, an actually good game. Avoid this.

Made it through the initial mode with each class, then beat the "traitor" path with a Brawler. The Brawler traitor path wasn't difficult, but it was a slog. Overall, if you enjoyed Fights in Tight spaces, you'll probably enjoy Knights in Tight Space. The game is fun, for a time. The addition of allies made for interesting strategies and combos which kept it interesting and enjoyable. The ability to leave the bounds of realism by switching to a fantasy setting (or at least further stretch the bounds of verisimilitude by adding magic to the universe) also added more flavor and variety. The larger maps make things less "tight space" like, but the inclusion of ranged opponents in those spaces sometimes kept the pressure of limited movement options that at least matched the spirit of "tight spaces." The story was generic, but that is fitting for the "Tight Spaces" style. There are points of genuine humor, though I don't recall anything resulting in true laughing out loud. I did appreciate it though. Side quests are worth doing, not necessarily for the rewards they give, but for the little story vignettes they represent. They're not Shakespeare, but they're entertaining (usually). Overall, I personally would rather play a game where my characters have a fixed set of abilities and I'm not dependent on RNG to determine what I will be able to do on any given turn. That said, for a card-based, grid-based, tactical combat game, it was fun.
